title: The Conciergerie and Marie Antoinette's Paris: what you see, and whether to add it to Sainte-Chapelle
subtitle: A medieval hall, a prison of the Revolution, and two quieter places in Paris where the same story ends.
excerpt: What the Conciergerie really shows of Marie Antoinette's last weeks, how long it takes, whether it is worth adding to Sainte-Chapelle next door, and where the story continues: the Expiatory Chapel and the royal tombs at Saint-Denis.
longtail_phrases: is the Conciergerie worth visiting
can you see Marie Antoinette's cell in the Conciergerie
how long does the Conciergerie take
should you visit the Conciergerie or Sainte-Chapelle
where is Marie Antoinette buried
meta_title: The Conciergerie and Marie Antoinette: is it worth it
meta_description: What the Conciergerie shows of Marie Antoinette's last weeks, how it pairs with Sainte-Chapelle, and the chapel and tombs where the story ends.

featured_image.alt: The long river front of the Conciergerie in Paris, with its round medieval towers and conical slate roofs above the Seine

content_html:
[place attraction="palais-de-la-cite" city="paris"]

In the night of 1 to 2 August 1793 Marie Antoinette was woken in the tower of the Temple, where the royal family had been held for a year, and driven across Paris to the Conciergerie. The register listed her as prisoner number 280, the Widow Capet. Her husband had been guillotined in January. Her son, eight years old, had been taken from her a month earlier.

She spent 76 days in a ground-floor cell, with gendarmes on watch behind a screen. On 14 October she was led upstairs to the Revolutionary Tribunal, which sat in the same building. The trial took two days. On the morning of 16 October a cart carried her to the square now called Place de la Concorde. She was 37. The Conciergerie is where Paris tells that story, and it stands a few steps from Sainte-Chapelle, which is what most visitors come to the island for. The question is whether to add it, and what you really see if you do.

What the building is

It is the oldest surviving part of the royal palace on the Île de la Cité. The kings of France lived here until the fourteenth century. After a revolt in 1358, Charles V moved out and left the palace to the courts and to a steward, the concierge, who also ran its prison. The name stayed. The prison closed only in 1914.

What you see inside

  • The Hall of the Men-at-Arms. Begun in 1302 under Philip the Fair, 64 metres long, four aisles of vaults on rows of pillars. It was the refectory for the two thousand or so people who served the palace, and it is one of the largest medieval halls left in Europe.
  • The kitchens, added around 1350, with a fireplace in each corner.
  • The prison rooms. The clerk's office where prisoners were entered in the register, the room where their hair was cut before the cart, and a room lined with the names of more than four thousand people tried by the Tribunal. More than 2,700 of them were sentenced to death.
  • The chapel of the Girondins, where by tradition twenty-one deputies spent their last night in October 1793.
  • The queen's chapel. In 1815 Louis XVIII, brother of Louis XVI, had the place of her cell turned into a memorial chapel. This is what stands on the spot today.
  • The Women's Courtyard, with its fountain and stone table, and the corner where condemned men waited to be called.

The Hall of the Men-at-Arms, begun in 1302: the dining hall of the palace staff. Photo: Chatsam, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

What you do not see is the cell as it was. Nothing in it survived the chapel. For many years a furnished reconstruction stood in the prison rooms, and displays here change, so do not count on a particular scene. The courtroom upstairs belongs to the law courts and is not part of the visit.

A reconstruction of the queen's cell, as the prison rooms showed it for many years. The real cell became a chapel. Photo: Pierre Poschadel, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

A tablet called the HistoPad shows the rooms as they looked in the Middle Ages and during the Revolution. It stops being handed out some time before closing.

How long, and the queue

Allow an hour to an hour and a half. The entrance is on Boulevard du Palais, with its own security check, separate from the one for Sainte-Chapelle a few doors along the same pavement. The line here is nearly always the shorter of the two. For hours and closing days, see our page for the Palais de la Cité.

The Women's Courtyard, where the women prisoners walked and washed their linen. Photo: Chatsam, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Is it worth adding to Sainte-Chapelle

The two are opposites. Sainte-Chapelle is half an hour of stained glass and needs no explaining. The Conciergerie is an hour of reading and imagining, in rooms with little in them.

  • Add it if the Revolution interests you, if it is raining, or if you want one great medieval room without a crowd.
  • Skip it with children under ten, or if you have one hour on the island: give that hour to the glass.
  • If you do both, go to Sainte-Chapelle first, at the time on your ticket, and to the Conciergerie afterwards. The monuments sell a combined ticket for the two. The partner's Conciergerie tickets cover the Conciergerie only.

What is free outside

Walk round to the Quai de l'Horloge. On the corner is the clock tower, which has carried a public clock since about 1370, the first in Paris. Its blue and gold dial dates from 1585. Along the quay stand three round towers of the old palace, best seen from the opposite bank.

Where the story continues

The Expiatory Chapel

The king and queen were buried without ceremony in the cemetery of the Madeleine, with hundreds of others guillotined on the same square. In January 1815 Louis XVIII had their remains dug up, and on the spot he built a chapel, finished in 1826. It stands in a small garden near Boulevard Haussmann. Inside are two marble groups, one of the king and one of the queen, with her last letter carved beneath hers. Half an hour is enough. It opens only on some days of the week: check our page for the Chapelle Expiatoire.

The Expiatory Chapel, built from 1815 over the cemetery where the king and queen were first buried. Photo: Thomon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Saint-Denis

The remains were taken to the Basilica of Saint-Denis, the burial church of the French kings, twenty minutes north of the centre on metro line 13. In 1793 its royal tombs had been opened and emptied. Today the king and queen lie in the crypt, and two kneeling marble statues of them stand in the church above. The nave is free. The tombs and the crypt need a ticket. Expect scaffolding on the west front, where the north spire is being rebuilt.

Louis XVI and Marie Antoinette at prayer, in the Basilica of Saint-Denis. Photo: Chabe01, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Conciergerie ticket lists entry and the HistoPad, and says plainly that Sainte-Chapelle is not included.
  • The Conciergerie ticket with an in-app audio tour adds a commentary on your own phone, inside and along the quay outside. There is no guide in person. Bring earphones.
  • The Expiatory Chapel ticket is entry only.
  • The Panthéon and Saint-Denis ticket pairs the tombs of the kings with the tombs of the Republic's great names, at opposite ends of Paris. Read on the listing how long it stays valid.

These are the tickets our partner sells for the Conciergerie and the two related sites, with today's prices:

[partner city="paris" match="conciergerie,expiatory,denis" limit="4"]

From here

Notre-Dame is five minutes away, at the other end of the island. Across the river in the Marais, the Carnavalet museum of the history of Paris keeps objects from the royal family's months in the Temple. See what else there is in Paris, or open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Dietmar Rabich, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the Conciergerie worth visiting?
faqs.a: Yes, if the French Revolution interests you or you want to see one of the largest medieval halls in Europe without a crowd. The rooms are bare and the visit depends on reading and on the tablet guide, so it suits adults better than small children.

faqs.q: Can you see Marie Antoinette's cell in the Conciergerie?
faqs.a: Not as it was. In 1815 the place of her cell was turned into a memorial chapel, which you visit. Reconstructions and displays about her imprisonment have changed over the years.

faqs.q: How long does the Conciergerie take?
faqs.a: An hour to an hour and a half. The line at its own security check is usually shorter than the one for Sainte-Chapelle next door.

faqs.q: Should you visit the Conciergerie or Sainte-Chapelle?
faqs.a: With a single hour, Sainte-Chapelle, for its stained glass. With two hours, both: Sainte-Chapelle first at your ticket time, then the Conciergerie. The partner's Conciergerie tickets do not include Sainte-Chapelle.

faqs.q: Where is Marie Antoinette buried?
faqs.a: In the crypt of the Basilica of Saint-Denis, north of Paris, where her remains and those of Louis XVI were taken in January 1815. The Expiatory Chapel in Paris marks the cemetery where they were first buried in 1793.

title: Villandry or Azay-le-Rideau from Tours: which château to choose, and how to get there without a car
subtitle: One is a garden with a château attached, the other a château on the water. One has a railway station, the other does not.
excerpt: The two châteaux west of Tours compared: what each visit is, how long it takes, how to reach Azay-le-Rideau by train and Villandry by bicycle, bus or minibus, and how to see both in one day without a car.
longtail_phrases: how to get to Villandry without a car
is there a train from Tours to Azay-le-Rideau
Villandry or Azay-le-Rideau which is better
can you visit Villandry and Azay-le-Rideau in one day
how far is Villandry from Tours by bike
meta_title: Villandry or Azay-le-Rideau from Tours without a car
meta_description: Villandry is gardens, Azay-le-Rideau is a château on the water. Which to choose from Tours, and how to reach each by train, bicycle or minibus.

featured_image.alt: The Château of Villandry with its square keep, above box hedges cut into patterns in the ornamental garden

content_html:
[place attraction="chateau-de-villandry" city="tours"]

In 1906 a Spanish doctor named Joachim Carvallo, who was doing medical research in Paris, bought a run-down château west of Tours with the fortune of his American wife, Ann Coleman. Villandry had been finished around 1536 for Jean Le Breton, a finance minister of François I, and was the last of the great Renaissance houses built along the Loire. By 1906 its grounds had been turned into a fashionable English-style park. Carvallo gave up his career, tore the park out, and spent the rest of his life rebuilding gardens of the sixteenth century from old engravings. His family still owns the place.

Twelve kilometres to the south, Azay-le-Rideau has a different founder's story. From 1518 Philippe Lesbahy ran the building site while her husband, Gilles Berthelot, a treasurer of the king, was away at court. In 1527 a cousin of his was hanged for embezzlement. Berthelot fled, never returned, and the king took the unfinished house. The two châteaux are close to each other and both lie west of Tours, so people try to see them together. Without a car that takes some planning, and it helps to know first which of the two you want more.

Two different visits

Villandry: the gardens

You come here for what is outside. The gardens climb the slope on three levels: a quiet water garden at the top, an ornamental garden in the middle where box hedges are cut into hearts, fans and flames, and at the bottom the kitchen garden, nine squares of vegetables planted for their colours and replanted twice a year. Around them are a maze, a herb garden and a newer garden of grasses and perennials. A belvedere and the top of the keep give the view from above, which is the one to have.

The house itself has furnished rooms of the eighteenth century and a carved and gilded Moorish ceiling that Carvallo brought in pieces from Toledo. There are two tickets: gardens only, or château and gardens. Allow two to three hours.

The ornamental garden from the belvedere: box cut into hearts, filled with flowers. Photo: Fab5669, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Box borders and standard roses in the kitchen garden, under the terraces. Photo: Nathalie Seigne, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Azay-le-Rideau: the building

Here the house is the sight. It stands on an island in the Indre, small, white and exactly mirrored in the water. Balzac, who lived nearby, called it a cut diamond set in the Indre. Its turrets are for show, not defence. The feature to look for is the grand staircase: straight flights behind open carved bays, in the Italian manner, when French houses still had spirals.

The state has owned Azay since 1905. After a restoration that ended in 2017, the rooms are furnished again and the oak roof timbers of the 1520s can be seen in the attic. One ticket covers the château and its park. Allow an hour and a half to two hours.

Azay-le-Rideau on its island in the Indre. Photo: Zairon, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The open bays of the grand staircase, on the courtyard side. Photo: Viaouest, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Which to choose

  • From May to September, and if you like gardens: Villandry. Nothing else in the Loire valley is like it.
  • In winter or in rain: Azay-le-Rideau. The clipped box at Villandry stays green all year, but the beds are bare and you are outdoors the whole time.
  • If you depend on public transport: Azay-le-Rideau, because it has a station.
  • If you have seen Chenonceau and Chambord: Villandry, for the change.

Azay-le-Rideau without a car

Regional trains on the line from Tours to Chinon stop at Azay-le-Rideau. The ride takes about half an hour. There are only a few a day, and some runs are replaced by a coach, so fix your return before you leave Tours. The station is on the edge of the village, about two kilometres from the château: a walk of twenty-five minutes, mostly downhill on the way there. There is no taxi rank.

The station of Azay-le-Rideau. The château is about two kilometres away. Photo: Spendeau, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Villandry without a car

Villandry has no station. The choices are these:

  • By bicycle. About twenty kilometres from Tours on the signposted Loire à Vélo route, flat, following the river Cher on paths and quiet roads. Bikes and electric bikes are hired in Tours. Count an hour and a half each way.
  • By bus. Buses from Tours to Villandry run on a few days of the week, with extra days in July and August. The timetable changes from year to year: ask at the tourist office in Tours before you plan around it.
  • By minibus tour. Half-day tours leave from the tourist office in Tours and pair the two châteaux in an afternoon, with about an hour at each. That is short for Villandry. Entry is normally paid on top.
  • By taxi. About twenty minutes from Tours. Book the return when you arrive.

Both in one day

The route that works without a car is by bicycle one way and train the other. Ride from Tours to Villandry in the morning and see the gardens. Ride on to Azay-le-Rideau, about twelve kilometres on small roads with one climb between the two valleys. Visit the château, then take a late afternoon train back to Tours with the bike. Regional trains carry bicycles, but places are limited: check when you buy the ticket.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Azay-le-Rideau entry ticket and the Villandry entry ticket are plain admissions. Neither includes transport or a guide. The details we could read do not say whether the Villandry ticket is for the gardens alone or for the château as well: check on the listing before you pay.
  • The partner files two more tickets under Tours. Chenonceau and Château Gaillard, a small royal estate in Amboise, both lie east of the city, in the opposite direction, and belong to another day.

These are the château tickets our partner sells around Tours, with today's prices:

[partner city="tours" match="villandry,azay" limit="4"]

From here

Langeais, on the Loire a few kilometres from Villandry, has a station of its own and a fortress with a working drawbridge in the middle of the town: see our page for the Château de Langeais. Current hours are on our pages for the Château de Villandry and the Château d'Azay-le-Rideau. Back in Tours, the half-timbered houses around Place Plumereau fill an evening, and the attractions map of France shows the rest of the valley.

Cover photo: Jean-Christophe Benoist, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.

faqs.q: How do you get to Villandry without a car?
faqs.a: By bicycle from Tours, about twenty flat kilometres on the Loire à Vélo route, by taxi, by a half-day minibus tour from the tourist office, or by a bus that runs only on some days. Villandry has no railway station.

faqs.q: Is there a train from Tours to Azay-le-Rideau?
faqs.a: Yes. Regional trains on the Tours to Chinon line take about half an hour, but there are only a few a day. The station is about two kilometres from the château.

faqs.q: Which is better, Villandry or Azay-le-Rideau?
faqs.a: They are different visits. Villandry is for its Renaissance gardens, best from May to September. Azay-le-Rideau is for the house itself, on an island in the Indre, and it works in any season.

faqs.q: Can you visit Villandry and Azay-le-Rideau in one day?
faqs.a: Yes. Without a car, ride a bicycle from Tours to Villandry and on to Azay-le-Rideau, about thirty-two kilometres in all, and take the train back. A half-day minibus tour also pairs them, with about an hour at each.

faqs.q: Do you need a ticket for the gardens of Villandry?
faqs.a: Yes. Villandry sells a gardens-only ticket and a ticket for the château and gardens together. Check which one a reseller is offering before you buy.

title: Vieux Lyon, the traboules and the climb to Fourvière: what is free and what needs a ticket
subtitle: Which doors to push in the old town, three ways up the hill, and the short list of things that cost money.
excerpt: A half-day in the old town of Lyon: how the traboules work and which ones to find, the cathedral, the funicular or the stairs to Fourvière, the basilica and the Roman theatres. Nearly all of it is free, and the partner sells audio walks, not tickets.
longtail_phrases: are the traboules in Lyon free
how to find the traboules in Vieux Lyon
how to get up to Fourvière from Vieux Lyon
is the Fourvière basilica free to enter
what is free to see in Lyon old town
meta_title: Vieux Lyon, traboules and Fourvière: free or ticket
meta_description: How the traboules of Vieux Lyon work and which to find, three ways up to Fourvière, and what in the old town of Lyon is free or needs a ticket.

featured_image.alt: The cathedral of Lyon on the bank of the Saône, with the white basilica of Fourvière and a metal tower on the hill behind it

content_html:
[place attraction="vieux-lyon" city="lyon"]

In the early 1960s the old town of Lyon was a slum, and the mayor wanted a road through it. The narrow strip of houses between the Saône and the hill of Fourvière had been the richest part of the city four centuries earlier, when Italian bankers, silk merchants and printers built their homes around its fairs. By 1960 the same houses were black with soot, crowded and without plumbing. A plan was drawn to clear a part of them for a wide road to a new bridge.

A group of residents fought it. In 1962 France passed a law, named after the culture minister André Malraux, that let whole districts be protected, and in May 1964 Vieux Lyon became the first in the country. The road was never built. In 1998 the quarter went onto the UNESCO list with the rest of historic Lyon. What was saved is some three hundred Renaissance houses, and the thing they are known for: the passages that run through them. Almost everything here is free, if you know which doors to push.

What a traboule is, and how to use one

The streets of Vieux Lyon run parallel to the river, and very few cross them. So people cut through the houses. A traboule is a corridor that enters one building from the street, crosses a courtyard or several, and comes out in the next street. The courtyards are the reward: spiral stair towers, galleries on three or four floors, old wells.

They are private property, and people live above them. The city has agreements with the owners of a few dozen, who keep the street doors unlocked during the day in return for help with the upkeep. That gives you these rules:

  • Go between mid-morning and early evening. Outside those hours the doors are locked.
  • Press the button beside the door, or simply push. If it does not open, it is not one of the public ones.
  • Keep your voice down, and stay off the stairs.

Four to find

  • The Long Traboule, from 54 Rue Saint-Jean to 27 Rue du Bœuf, through four houses and their courtyards.
  • 27 Rue Saint-Jean to 6 Rue des Trois-Maries.
  • The Tour Rose, at 16 Rue du Bœuf: a courtyard with a round pink stair tower, not a passage through.
  • 2 Place du Gouvernement to the quay on the Saône.

One of the courtyards of the Long Traboule, between Rue Saint-Jean and Rue du Bœuf. Photo: Chabe01, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

The round stair tower called the Tour Rose, in a courtyard off Rue du Bœuf. Photo: Fred Romero, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

The rest of the old town, for free

The Cathedral of Saint-Jean was built between 1180 and 1480, and you can read the three centuries in it, from the round-arched apse to the Gothic front. Henri IV married Marie de' Medici here in 1600. Entry is free. Inside is an astronomical clock whose oldest parts go back to the fourteenth century.

From the cathedral, Rue Saint-Jean runs north to Place du Change, where the money changers worked. Rue du Bœuf, one street up the slope, is quieter and has the better courtyards.

Three ways up to Fourvière

  • The funicular. It leaves from inside the Vieux Lyon metro station, beside the cathedral. There are two lines: one to Fourvière, for the basilica, and one that stops at Minimes, for the Roman theatres. It takes an ordinary city transport ticket, so a day pass covers it. It closes for a short maintenance break most years, and buses replace it.
  • The stairs. The Montée des Chazeaux climbs 228 steps straight up from Rue du Bœuf. From its top a path through the Rosary Gardens goes on to the basilica. About twenty-five minutes, and steep.
  • The sensible mix. Ride up, walk down.

At the top

In October 1870, with the Prussian army advancing through France, the Catholics of Lyon vowed to build a church to the Virgin if the city was spared. It was, and the Basilica of Notre-Dame de Fourvière went up between 1872 and 1884, paid for by donations. There are two churches, one above the other, covered in mosaic. Entry is free. Guided visits to the roof are sold separately, in season.

The esplanade beside it is the best view of Lyon: both rivers, the red roofs, and on a clear day Mont Blanc on the horizon. The metal tower next door is a television mast and cannot be visited.

Lyon from the esplanade of Fourvière. The view is free. Photo: Mathieudu68, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

Ten minutes' walk south are the Roman theatres. Lyon was founded up here in 43 BC, as Lugdunum, and the larger theatre, begun about 15 BC, is the oldest in France. A smaller one for music stands beside it. You walk the tiers freely during the day. In June and July a festival puts a stage and seating over part of the stones.

The Roman theatre on the hill, begun about 15 BC. The site is open without a ticket. Photo: Pymouss, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What needs a ticket

  • the funicular fare;
  • the Lugdunum museum, built into the hillside beside the theatres;
  • the Gadagne museums, on the history of Lyon and on puppets, in a Renaissance mansion in the old town;
  • the museum of film sets and miniatures on Rue Saint-Jean;
  • the roof visit at the basilica.

None of them is needed for the walk. Choose one if it rains.

What the partner sells

For this part of Lyon the partner has no entry tickets, because there is almost nothing to enter. It sells three self-guided audio walks, played in its app on your own phone:

  • one through Vieux Lyon and its passages, starting in front of the cathedral, about two hours;
  • one from Place Bellecour up to the basilica and the Roman theatre, listed at an hour and a half, which is brisk for that climb;
  • one through the old quarter by its stories, about two hours.

The listings say that tickets along the way are not included and that no guide comes with you. Bring earphones.

These are the audio walks and tickets our partner sells in Lyon, with today's prices:

[partner city="lyon" match="vieux,stones,time" limit="3"]

From here

Across the Saône, the slopes of the Croix-Rousse have traboules of another kind, built for the silk weavers of the nineteenth century, taller and plainer. Between the two rivers lie Place Bellecour and Place des Terreaux. For hours, see our pages for Vieux Lyon and the Roman theatre of Fourvière, look at the rest of Lyon, or open the trip planner for France.

Cover photo: Chris 73, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.

faqs.q: Are the traboules in Lyon free?
faqs.a: Yes. The public ones are open during the day without charge, under agreements between the city and the owners. They are private buildings where people live, so visitors are asked to be quiet and to stay off the stairs.

faqs.q: How do you find the traboules in Vieux Lyon?
faqs.a: Start with the Long Traboule, from 54 Rue Saint-Jean to 27 Rue du Bœuf, then 27 Rue Saint-Jean and the Tour Rose courtyard at 16 Rue du Bœuf. Press the button beside the door or push: if it does not open, it is not a public one.

faqs.q: How do you get up to Fourvière from Vieux Lyon?
faqs.a: By the funicular from the Vieux Lyon metro station, with an ordinary city transport ticket, or on foot by the 228 steps of the Montée des Chazeaux and the path through the Rosary Gardens, in about twenty-five minutes.

faqs.q: Is the Fourvière basilica free to enter?
faqs.a: Yes. Entry to the basilica and its lower church is free, and so is the view from the esplanade. Guided visits to the roof are sold separately.

faqs.q: What is free to see in the old town of Lyon?
faqs.a: The traboules, the Cathedral of Saint-Jean, the streets and courtyards of the Renaissance quarter, the basilica of Fourvière, the view from its esplanade and the Roman theatres on the hill.

title: Amsterdam Noord by the free ferry: is A'DAM Lookout worth it, and what else is across the water
subtitle: Five minutes by boat behind Centraal Station: a tower with a swing, a flight film, and a good deal that costs nothing.
excerpt: How the free ferry behind Amsterdam Centraal works, what the A'DAM Lookout ticket gives you and whether it is worth it, what THIS IS HOLLAND is, and what you can see in Amsterdam Noord without paying.
longtail_phrases: is A'DAM Lookout worth it
is the ferry to Amsterdam Noord free
is the swing included in the A'DAM Lookout ticket
what is THIS IS HOLLAND in Amsterdam
what to do in Amsterdam Noord for free
meta_title: Amsterdam Noord by free ferry: is A'DAM Lookout worth it
meta_description: The free ferry behind Centraal Station, what the A'DAM Lookout ticket and its swing give you, THIS IS HOLLAND, and what is free in Amsterdam Noord.

featured_image.alt: A blue and white ferry on the IJ in Amsterdam in front of the dark A'DAM tower and the white EYE film museum

content_html:
[place attraction="eye-filmmuseum" city="amsterdam"]

For most of Amsterdam's history, the far bank of the IJ was where the city put what it did not want to see. The spit of land opposite the harbour was the gallows field. People were executed on Dam Square, and their bodies were rowed across and left on display, as a warning to every ship that came in. In May 1664 Rembrandt crossed the water to draw one of them: Elsje Christiaens, a Danish girl of eighteen who had killed her landlady with an axe. His two drawings of her are now in New York.

Later the bank filled with shipyards and with the laboratories of Shell, which in 1971 added an office tower set at an angle to the water. Shell moved out in 2009. In 2016 the tower reopened as A'DAM, with bars, a hotel, and an observation deck on the roof. The north bank is now five minutes from Centraal Station by a ferry that costs nothing. What you spend when you land is up to you, and the question most people have is whether the tower is worth its ticket.

The ferry

Walk through Centraal Station to the side that faces the water. The ferries of the city transport company leave from the quay there. They are free, for people on foot and on bicycles alike. There is no ticket and no gate. You walk on.

  • To Buiksloterweg: the short crossing, straight over, in about five minutes. It runs every few minutes through the day, and all night at longer intervals. It lands beside the EYE film museum and the tower.
  • To NDSM: a longer ride west along the harbour, about a quarter of an hour, a few times an hour. It lands at the former shipyard.

The crossing is a small harbour trip in itself. Stand at the front on the way over and at the back on the way home, when the old city is in front of you.

The ferry in mid-crossing in 2015, when the tower was still being rebuilt. Photo: Guilhem Vellut, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.

A'DAM Lookout: what the ticket is

A lift takes you to the twentieth floor in well under a minute, with a light show on the way. There is an indoor level with windows all round and a bar, and above it the open roof, about a hundred metres up. The view is a full circle: the IJ and the back of the station to the south, with the church towers of the old city behind it, the port to the west, and to the north the flat green polder with its villages.

On the edge of the roof is the swing, which carries you out over the side of the building and back. It is not part of the standard entry: it is paid as a supplement, and there is a minimum height. Plan on forty-five minutes to an hour in all. The deck stays open into the evening, and the hour before sunset is the busiest.

The view south from the deck: the IJ, Centraal Station and the old city behind it. Photo: Alexis Jazz, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0.

The swing on the roof edge. It is a supplement, not part of every ticket. Photo: Muck, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Is it worth it

  • Yes, on a clear day. Amsterdam is flat and low, and has very few places where the public can get this high. The view over the water and the harbour is the one you cannot have anywhere else.
  • Yes, at dusk, if you book that slot ahead.
  • No, under low cloud. The city turns to grey on grey.
  • No, if you want the canals from above. The canal ring is more than a kilometre away and hidden between its own roofs. From here you see towers, not water.

If you would sooner not pay, the ferry gives you the skyline from the water, and the steps and terrace of the film museum face the same way. Back on the city side, the sloping roof of the NEMO science museum has long been open as a free terrace: check before you count on it.

THIS IS HOLLAND

The round building at the foot of the tower holds one attraction. You sit in a row of hanging seats in front of a curved screen and are lifted into a film that flies over the Netherlands: bulb fields, dikes, windmills, the tidal flats of the Wadden Sea, the canals of Amsterdam. The seats tilt, and wind, mist and scents are added. Short films before it explain how the country was made out of water. The whole visit takes about an hour, and the flight itself only a few minutes.

It is a ride, not a museum. It suits families, a wet afternoon, and visitors who will see nothing of the country beyond Amsterdam. It does not suit people who get motion sick, and there is a minimum height for children.

What is free in Noord

  • The EYE film museum. The white building of 2012 is free to walk into: the tiered hall, the café and the terrace on the water. Exhibitions and film screenings have tickets.
  • The NDSM wharf. A shipyard until 1984, now cranes, slipways, painted walls and a huge shed of studios. Walking about is free. The street art museum there has a ticket.
  • The dike villages. A quarter of an hour north by bicycle, the Nieuwendammerdijk is a row of old wooden houses along a dike.

A crane of the former NDSM shipyard, a quarter of an hour away by the second ferry. Photo: Steven Lek, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Reading the partner's listings

  • A'DAM Lookout, fast track ticket with a drink: entry by the shorter lane, and a drink at the bar. The title says one drink and the description two: go by what the listing shows on the day.
  • Entry ticket with a burger menu: entry, and a burger with fries in the tower.
  • Entry ticket with lunch or dinner at Madam: entry, and a deposit towards your bill at the restaurant on the tower. You pay the rest there.
  • THIS IS HOLLAND, entry ticket: one showing of the flight.

The descriptions of the tower tickets mention the swing as something you can do there, without saying it is included. Assume it is a supplement unless the listing says otherwise.

These are the tickets our partner sells for A'DAM Lookout and THIS IS HOLLAND, with today's prices:

[partner city="amsterdam" match="lookout,holland" limit="4"]

A half day in order

Take the NDSM ferry in the middle of the afternoon and walk the wharf. Come back along the bank by bicycle, or by the ferries by way of the station, to the film museum. Go up the tower an hour before sunset, then take the short ferry back with the lights of the city ahead of you.

From here

The short ferry puts you back at Centraal Station, ten minutes on foot from Dam Square. For films and exhibitions, see our page for the EYE Filmmuseum. The rest of the city is on our page for Amsterdam, and the trip planner for the Netherlands fits it into a longer route.

Cover photo: Marion Golsteijn, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

faqs.q: Is the ferry to Amsterdam Noord free?
faqs.a: Yes. The city ferries from the water side of Centraal Station are free for people on foot and on bicycles, with no ticket. The crossing to Buiksloterweg takes about five minutes and runs day and night.

faqs.q: Is A'DAM Lookout worth it?
faqs.a: On a clear day or at dusk, yes: it is one of the few high public viewpoints in a flat city, and the only one over the harbour. Under low cloud it is not, and it does not show the canals from above.

faqs.q: Is the swing included in the A'DAM Lookout ticket?
faqs.a: Not in the standard entry. The swing over the edge of the roof is paid as a supplement, and it has a minimum height. Check what a ticket lists before you buy.

faqs.q: What is THIS IS HOLLAND in Amsterdam?
faqs.a: A flight simulator film in the round building beside the tower. You sit in hanging seats before a curved screen and fly over the Netherlands, with wind, mist and scents. The visit takes about an hour.

faqs.q: What can you do in Amsterdam Noord for free?
faqs.a: Ride the ferries, walk into the EYE film museum and sit on its terrace, wander the former NDSM shipyard, and cycle to the wooden houses of the Nieuwendammerdijk.

title: Rotterdam to Kinderdijk by waterbus: which boat, how long, and what the windmill ticket covers
subtitle: Half an hour on a public ferry, a flat walk between nineteen windmills, and a ticket you may not need.
excerpt: How to reach the windmills of Kinderdijk from Rotterdam by waterbus: where the boat leaves, how long it takes, what you can walk for free, what the Kinderdijk ticket adds, and what the partner's waterbus tickets do and do not include.

meta_description: Where the waterbus to Kinderdijk leaves in Rotterdam, how long it takes, what you can walk for free, and what the windmill ticket really adds.

featured_image.alt: A row of windmills at Kinderdijk reflected in a canal edged with reeds and water lilies

content_html:
[place attraction="kinderdijk-windmills" city="rotterdam"]

In the night of 18 to 19 November 1421, a storm tide broke the dikes of South Holland. The flood, named after Saint Elizabeth, whose feast day it was, drowned whole villages and left an inland sea. The story told ever since is that when the water began to fall, people standing on a dike saw a wooden cradle drifting towards them. A cat was jumping from one side of it to the other to keep it level. Inside, a baby was asleep, and dry. The place was called Kinderdijk, the children's dike.

The land behind that dike lies lower than the rivers around it, and has been kept dry by ditches, sluices and pumps since the Middle Ages. In 1738 and 1740 the two local water boards built sixteen large windmills in two rows to lift the water in steps towards the river. With three others nearby, nineteen still stand. Steam took over their work in 1868, but they were kept ready, and were used again in the Second World War when there was no fuel. UNESCO listed them in 1997. From Rotterdam, the pleasant way to reach them is by water.

Which boat

The Waterbus is public transport: fast catamarans that run on the rivers between Rotterdam and Dordrecht. In Rotterdam they leave from the jetty on Willemskade, at the foot of the Erasmus Bridge on the city side, a few minutes on foot from Leuvehaven metro station.

  • The direct boat goes from the Erasmus Bridge to Kinderdijk in about half an hour. Out of season it sails less often and can start late in the morning.
  • The Dordrecht boat is the other way. You get off at Ridderkerk, on the opposite bank, and a small ferry takes you across to Kinderdijk. It is slower, with a change, and useful when the direct boat is not running.

Line numbers and timetables have changed in recent years, so do not rely on an old blog post. Read the board on the jetty, and note the time of the last boat back before you walk away from the landing stage. Bicycles are carried. In good weather sit on the open deck at the back.

Do not confuse it with the harbour cruises that leave from the same quay, or with the small yellow water taxis.

A waterbus leaving the Erasmus Bridge jetty in Rotterdam. Photo: AgainErick, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What you can walk for free

From the landing stage it is five minutes to the entrance. Beyond it, a long straight path for walkers and cyclists runs between the two rows of mills, with a canal on either side. It is a public path. You can walk it without a ticket and see every mill from the outside, which is how they are best seen.

  • On one side stand the eight round brick mills of 1738.
  • On the other, the eight-sided thatched ones of 1740.
  • To the far end and back is about four kilometres, flat, with no shade and no shelter. Bring a jacket even in summer: it is windy, which is why the mills are here.

The round brick mills of 1738, seen from the public path. Photo: Michielverbeek, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

What the windmill ticket covers

The ticket sold by Kinderdijk itself is for going inside. It includes:

  • Two museum mills. One of the round brick mills is furnished as the home of a miller's large family, with box beds built into the walls around the turning shaft. The other is an older and smaller type, with its yard and vegetable plot. The ladders are steep and the rooms are tiny.
  • The pumping stations. The Wisboom station of 1868, with its machinery and a film, and the visitor centre.
  • The canal boats that run along the mills. They sail in the main season, so in winter the ticket gives you less.

It does not include your transport from Rotterdam.

The canal boat, which is part of the ticket, passing the mills. Photo: Paul van Galen, Rijksdienst voor het Cultureel Erfgoed, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Inside the Wisboom pumping station, built in 1868 to do the work of the mills. Photo: Karmakolle, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Do you need it

  • Yes if you want to stand inside a working mill and see how a family lived in one, or if you are with children, who get more from the boat and the inside of a mill than from the walk.
  • No if you have two hours and came for the landscape. The path gives you that.

Either way, allow two to three hours on the spot, and half a day from Rotterdam and back.

Reading the partner's listings

  • The Waterbus ticket between Rotterdam and Kinderdijk is a boat ticket bought ahead. The details we could read list nothing more, so treat it as transport only, and check on the listing whether it covers the return.
  • The Waterbus ticket with audio city walks adds self-guided audio routes in the partner's app, for Rotterdam and for Kinderdijk. The listing states that tickets to attractions on the way are not included. The entry to the museum mills is therefore extra, bought at Kinderdijk.
  • The Rotterdam audio walks are commentary only, on your own phone: the old centre from the City Hall to the old harbour, the port, the modern architecture from the Markthal to the Erasmus Bridge, and the bombing of 1940. One of them mentions a water taxi ride that is paid separately. Bring earphones.

These are the waterbus tickets and audio walks our partner sells in Rotterdam, with today's prices:

[partner city="rotterdam" match="waterbus,audio,walk" limit="6"]

When to go

Take the first direct boat. River cruise ships and coaches arrive from late morning, and the path is narrow. The mills do not turn every day: on some summer days all of them are set going, and the dates are announced by the site. In the afternoon the light falls on the brick mills, and in the morning on the thatched ones. Current hours are on our page for the Kinderdijk windmills.

From here

The Waterbus carries on upriver to Dordrecht, the oldest city of Holland, with a harbour quarter worth an hour or two before the boat back. In Rotterdam, the jetty is under the Erasmus Bridge, and the Euromast tower is twenty minutes' walk along the river. See the rest of Rotterdam, or open the trip planner for the Netherlands.

Cover photo: Tarod, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 NL.

faqs.q: How do you get from Rotterdam to Kinderdijk by boat?
faqs.a: By Waterbus from the jetty on Willemskade, at the foot of the Erasmus Bridge. A direct boat goes to Kinderdijk. When it is not running, take the Dordrecht boat to Ridderkerk and the small ferry across.

faqs.q: How long is the waterbus from Rotterdam to Kinderdijk?
faqs.a: About half an hour on the direct boat. The route with a change at Ridderkerk takes longer. Check the time of the last boat back when you arrive.

faqs.q: Is Kinderdijk free to walk around?
faqs.a: Yes. The path between the two rows of windmills is public, and you can walk or cycle it without a ticket and see all the mills from outside. The ticket is for the insides and the boats.

faqs.q: What does the Kinderdijk ticket include?
faqs.a: Entry to two museum mills, the Wisboom pumping station with its film, the visitor centre, and in season the boats along the canal. It does not include transport from Rotterdam.

faqs.q: How much time do you need at Kinderdijk?
faqs.a: Two to three hours on the spot. The walk to the far mills and back is about four kilometres. With the waterbus from Rotterdam, count half a day.
